MUJAHID:v2p776#3/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p776#3/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p776#3/r1.claim: Mujahid says the early raiders are horses in battle.

MUJAHID:v2p776#3/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p776#3/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
MUJAHID:v2p776#3/r2.claim: A report from Ibn Masud says the early raiders are horses during pilgrimage.

MUJAHID:v2p776#4/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p776#4/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p776#4/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses the horses' arrival among a group as these and those.

MUQATIL:100:1-6/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:100:1-6/r5.speaker: مقاتل
MUQATIL:100:1-6/r5.claim: The horses attack the enemy at dawn.

FARRA:v3p284#2/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p284#2/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p284#2/r4.claim: The horses raided at dawn in an expedition sent by the Messenger to Banu Kinana; revelation reported its delayed news.

FARRA:v3p284#2/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p284#2/r5.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
FARRA:v3p284#2/r5.claim: Ali instead identifies the chargers as camels and connects the oath to Badr, when only al-Miqdad's horse was present.

TAB-FULL:v24p572/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p572/r6.speaker: ابن عباس وعلي
TAB-FULL:v24p572/r6.claim: In a conversation with Ali, Ibn Abbas first says the oath concerns horses raiding for God's cause and lighting cooking fires at night; Ali counters that Badr had only two horses and identifies the creatures as pilgrims' camels moving from Arafat through Muzdalifa to Mina, and Ibn Abbas recants.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the morning raiders are horses attacking in God's cause.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r2.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r2.claim: Ikrima says they attack the enemy at daybreak.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r3.claim: Mujahid identifies the morning raiders as horses.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r4.claim: Qatadah says the horses attack their enemy after morning begins.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r5.claim: Ibn Masud says the verse refers to camels as pilgrims leave Jam for Mina on the day of sacrifice.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r6.claim: Al-Tabari includes every creature that raids in the morning because the wording does not specify one raider over another.

TAB-FULL:v24p579/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r7.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
TAB-FULL:v24p579/r7.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam used to decline interpreting these letters and said they form an oath sworn by God.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3457#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3457#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3457#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says horses raid at dawn, kick up dust from their hoof marks, and reach the enemy group.

NAHHAS:v5p277/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r13.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v5p277/r13.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the raiders as horses.

NAHHAS:v5p277/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r14.speaker: ابن مسعود
NAHHAS:v5p277/r14.claim: Ibn Masud identifies the raiders as camels.

THALABI:v10p270/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r10.speaker: القرظي
THALABI:v10p270/r10.claim: He says they are camels rushing with their riders from Jamʿ to Mina on the Day of Sacrifice; the rite delays departure until morning, and ghāra means to travel quickly.

THALABI:v10p270/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r11.speaker: أبو حيوة
THALABI:v10p270/r11.claim: He reads fa-aththarna with a doubled consonant, meaning the beasts leave an impact at the place they reach, omitted from the wording because it is understood.

THALABI:v10p270/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r9.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v10p270/r9.claim: Most exegetes identify the dawn raiders as horses carrying their riders against the enemy at daybreak.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas says cavalry raid the enemy at dawn, when their attack is visible like the rising morning.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r12.speaker: علي
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r12.claim: Ali says the camels run in the morning from Muzdalifah to Mina.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327/r1.claim: The following Sūrat al-Qāriʿah is Meccan according to all the authorities mentioned.

QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r9.claim: The attackers raid the enemy in the morning.

WAHIDI-QT:100:3/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:100:3/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:100:3/r1.claim: The horses raid the enemy at dawn; although their riders do the raiding, the speech is attributed to the horses.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r3.claim: They raid the enemy at dawn; the wording assigns riders' action to their mounts.

JISHUMI:v10p7511/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r1.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة وقتادة
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r1.claim: Al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, and Qatadah say the surah is Meccan; another view says it is Medinan and was revealed around a raid.

JISHUMI:v10p7511/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r2.claim: A report promises ten good deeds for reciting the surah for every person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r14.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r14.claim: These descriptions are the objects of the oath.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r6.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r6.claim: Most commentators identify the raiders at dawn as horses and their riders charging the enemy in the morning.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r7.speaker: القرظي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r7.claim: Al-Qurazi offers camels and riders departing Muzdalifa for Mina on the Day of Sacrifice; the pilgrimage practice is to wait until dawn.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r8.claim: The verb al-ighara means to travel quickly, as in the saying that Thabir should shine so that the travelers may depart.

KASHSHAF:100:3/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:100:3/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:100:3/r1.claim: The raiders attack the enemy at dawn.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p795/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p795/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p795/r8.claim: A report promises ten good deeds for reciting al-ʿĀdiyāt for every person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r6.speaker: علي وابن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r6.claim: Ali and Ibn Masud take the morning raiders as camels moving from Muzdalifah to Mina or at Badr.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وجماعة كثيرة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas and many others identify the raiders as horses, in God's campaigns or other journeys; raids commonly began at dawn after night travel.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r8.claim: The verb aghara can mean charging or running.

TABRISI:100:1-4/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1-4/r12.speaker: الأكثرون
TABRISI:100:1-4/r12.claim: Most say the horses attack at dawn because riders travel through the night.

TABRISI:100:1-4/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1-4/r13.speaker: محمد بن كعب
TABRISI:100:1-4/r13.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb instead says camels rise from Jamʿ to Minā on Sacrifice morning.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p206#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p206#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p206#2/r5.claim: In the expedition account, the horses snort through their nostrils, spark with their hooves on stones, attack at dawn, raise dust, and reach the enemy together.

RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r5.claim: The camels’ morning raid is their rapid movement as pilgrims hurry from Muzdalifah to Mina on the morning of the sacrifice.

RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r9.speaker: أبي عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r9.claim: A report attributed to Ubay and raised to the Prophet promises a reward measured by the number who spend a night at Muzdalifah and witness Jamʿ.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p61/r8.claim: Mentioning dawn signals the horse’s exhaustion and full exertion; its persistence models how a servant should continue obeying God despite weakness.

RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r1.claim: The default reading is horses attacking an enemy at dawn: it is too dark to see at night, while people are ready for battle during the day and inattentive at dawn.

RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r2.claim: Those who take the animals as camels say they carry pilgrims from Muzdalifa to Mina on the Sacrifice day, when the rite requires waiting until morning; إغارة means speed.

RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r3.speaker: العرب
RAZI-FULL:v32p62#2/r3.claim: The pre-Islamic Arabs said, Rise, Thabir, so that we may hasten onward, illustrating the sense of swift departure.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas and most commentators say the horses raid the enemy at dawn, after traveling secretly by night when people are unwary.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r2.claim: Dawn is the moment of surprise because people are heedless; the Qur'an says a warning people's morning was disastrous.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r3.claim: Another reading says their strength let them raid openly by day, with morning serving as a simile for visibility.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود وعلي
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r4.claim: Ibn Mas'ud and Ali say these are camels carrying riders from Mina toward Muzdalifa on the Day of Sacrifice; al-Qurazi says they should not leave before daybreak.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:3/r5.claim: Ighara means traveling swiftly, as in the instruction that Mount Thabir shine so the pilgrims may depart quickly.

BAYDAWI-FULL:100:1-5/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:100:1-5/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:100:1-5/r4.claim: The raiders attack the enemy in the morning.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#3/r1.claim: The raiders attack the enemy in the morning.

QASHANI:100:1-4/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:100:1-4/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:100:1-4/r4.claim: The souls abandon outer material attachments and inner dispositions, deeds, desires, pleasures, and imaginings by the light of divine manifestation.

QASHANI:100:1-4/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:100:1-4/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:100:1-4/r5.claim: This stripping away occurs through dawn-like divine manifestation, its first signs, renunciation, and detachment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p526/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p526/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p526/r8.claim: Aghāra means attacking an enemy to plunder, kill, or capture.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r7.claim: The raiders attack the enemy at dawn; for camel interpreters the word can mean running fast from Muzdalifa to Mina or at Badr.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r1.claim: ‘Subhan’ is a time adverb meaning at dawn; aghara means to raid by surprise for plunder, killing, or capture, and a poem witnesses the raid sense.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r2.claim: Ghara or aghara can also mean descending into a low valley; this is a rare dialectal usage.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r3.claim: One view takes all the racing, sparking, and raiding descriptions as horses; their descriptions are coordinated in sequence as in a cited poetic example.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r4.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r4.claim: A view attributed to the Commander of the Faithful takes the descriptions as camels running from ‘Arafa to Muzdalifa and Mina; a poem by Safiyya bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib supports this interpretation.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r5.claim: Some interpret ‘al-muriyat’ as a group scheming in war; the idiom ‘I will light you up’ means ‘I will plot against you’.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r2.claim: The Prophet used to raid at dawn and listen for the call to prayer; if it was heard he held back, otherwise he attacked.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah say the horses raid at dawn in God's cause; those who read the oath as camels take this as the morning journey from Muzdalifah to Mina.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r4.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says the Prophet sent horses on an expedition and heard no news for a month; the surah then revealed, and al-Bazzar calls the report very unusual.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r12.claim: The horses carry their riders into a raid against the enemy, driving hard to kill and plunder.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r13.claim: A raid is most terrifying when it comes at the end of night.

DURR-FULL:v8p600/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r13.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r13.claim: The attack occurs when the horses reach the enemy in the morning and penetrate their ranks.

DURR-FULL:v8p600/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r3.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r3.claim: They attack the enemy in the morning.

DURR-FULL:v8p600/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r9.claim: The cavalry raids and surprises the enemy in the morning.

DURR-FULL:v8p601/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas says the horses attack the enemy in the morning.

DURR-FULL:v8p601/r19.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r19.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r19.claim: The horses raid in the morning.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r11.speaker: عطية
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r11.claim: Atiyya identifies the dawn raiders as horses.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r2.claim: Qatada reads the passage as horses running until panting, striking sparks with their hooves, raiding at dawn, raising dust, entering the people’s gathering; kanud means ungrateful.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r22.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r22.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r22.claim: Ibn Masud places the morning departure at the pilgrims’ movement from Muzdalifah.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r5.claim: Mujahid identifies the morning raiders as horses.

BURSEVI:v10p383/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p383/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p383/r6.claim: The raid is the surprise attack on an enemy for plunder, killing, or capture; the action is attributed to the horses because they are central to the mounted raid.

BURSEVI:v10p383/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p383/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p383/r7.claim: The horses attack at dawn, the customary time for a raid: they travel unseen at night and strike while the enemy is unaware; “O morning!” warns of such danger.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r1.claim: Mughīrāt are horses whose riders attack an enemy suddenly for plunder, killing, or capture; the action is attributed to the horses figuratively or with an omitted أصحاب.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r2.claim: Ṣubḥan is an adverb meaning at daybreak, the customary time for raids prepared under cover of night.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#3/r3.claim: The cited poem celebrates a people who began a relentless raid at daybreak.

ELMALILI:100:3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:3/r1.claim: Mughirāt can mean raiders moving swiftly, attacking, or plundering, and can also mean entering low-lying land; in common usage it chiefly means a raid or surprise attack.

ELMALILI:100:3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:3/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:3/r2.claim: Some take the verse as camels hurrying pilgrims to Mina in the morning, but enemy-raiding cavalry is the more immediate meaning.

ELMALILI:100:3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:3/r3.claim: A dawn raid allows attackers to prepare unseen overnight and then see clearly, reducing mistakes; although night raids sometimes succeed, they are more dangerous.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r1.claim: The Meccan surah has eleven verses and moves in rapid, forceful jumps before settling at its ending, like a runner reaching the finish.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r2.claim: The opening scene shows charging, panting horses striking sparks, attacking at dawn, raising dust, and suddenly breaking into enemy ranks.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r6.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r6.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r6.claim: The rough, rumbling, cracking rhythm suits the noisy dust and forceful disclosure of graves and hearts, as well as the surah’s ingratitude and greed.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r7.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r7.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r7.claim: The oath’s noisy cavalry scene frames the surah’s moral and resurrection scenes: image and frame mirror one another.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:3/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:3/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:3/r1.claim: The raiding horses attack early in the morning to take the enemy by surprise.

IBNASHUR:100:3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:100:3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:100:3/r1.claim: Al-mughirat is the active participle of aghara, usually meaning to raid a people's home; attributing the raid to the horses is figurative because the riders raid and the horses are their means.

IBNASHUR:100:3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:100:3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:100:3/r2.claim: Ighara can also mean rushing forward in travel.

IBNASHUR:100:3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:100:3/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:100:3/r3.claim: Subhan is a time adverb; if the referent is raiding cavalry, dawn is specified because they attacked after daybreak, as reflected in the warning cry and the cited verse.

IBNASHUR:100:3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:100:3/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:100:3/r4.claim: Alternatively, the referent is camels rushing from Muzdalifa to Mina on Sacrifice day, departing when the sun shone on Thabir, as in the saying addressed to the mountain.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r1.claim: Al-Mughirat derives from raid; attributing the riders' raiding to their mounts is a rational trope because horses or camels are its means, though it can also mean rushing along.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r2.claim: For warhorses, the raid occurs at dawn because raids began after daybreak, prompting the warning cry ya sabahah.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r3.claim: For racing pilgrimage camels, the phrase means departing Muzdalifa for Mina on the morning of the sacrifice, as the sun rose over Thabir.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r4.claim: The saying 'Rise, Thabir, so we may depart' refers to that pilgrimage movement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r9.claim: The carefully chosen words accommodate both warhorses and pilgrimage camels, a feature of the surah's rhetorical arrangement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p501/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p501/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p501/r1.claim: The first three descriptions are joined by fa, the usual Arabic pattern for successive adjectives or places; it usually marks sequential occurrence here and in Ibn Ziyaba's verse, but may mark mention order in al-Saffat.

TABATABAI:100:1-5/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r8.claim: Ighārah is a surprise cavalry attack; the verse attributes the riders' action to their horses.

TABATABAI:100:1-5/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r9.claim: An alternative pictures camels rising from Jamʿ to Minā at dawn; taking raid to mean quick movement is contrary to the apparent sense.

BINTSHATI:v1p107/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r3.claim: Arabic associates a raid with horses even when they are not named; to raid is to unleash horses, and a horse raids by accelerating, supporting this interpretation.

BINTSHATI:v1p107/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r4.claim: Dawn specifies surprise because the enemy is unprepared and unaware; al-Tibyān and Muḥammad ʿAbduh make the same point.

BINTSHATI:v1p107/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r5.claim: Arabic uses morning as a raid day, and Qur'anic morning, dawn, and early-day language often signals surprise and warning, as in cited destruction passages.

BINTSHATI:v1p108/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p108/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p108/r1.claim: Further examples of morning surprise and warning include the destruction passages at 54:38, 7:78, and 11:81, alongside the other listed verses.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p416/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p416/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p416/r4.claim: Dawn was the preferred time for Arabian raids; the alarm wa ṣabāḥā reflects this, and ṣabāḥ became a common term for plunder.

STUDYQURAN:100:1/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:100:1/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:100:1/r4.claim: Pilgrimage camels rush from Mashʿar to Minā at dawn on the Day of Sacrifice.
